paragraphs: The paper studies how to summarize a network through hidden properties of its nodes. Simple network models assign nodes to groups and explain links through those assignments. Allowing groups to overlap adds flexibility, but both overlapping and disjoint groupings can still describe relationships at only one level.

The proposed model adds a second layer of structure. Each object has a vector of latent features, and each feature is further divided into distinct subgroups. This lets the model represent differences within a shared attribute, rather than treating every object with that attribute as equivalent. A hierarchical Bayesian formulation provides the framework for these nested relationships.

In experiments on social and biological networks, the model substantially improves prediction of links. These results support the authors' view that a single hierarchical layer can oversimplify real network structure. The contribution is therefore both a richer representation of relationships and empirical evidence that the extra structure can help predict connections.
icml-2012-an-infinite-latent-attribute-m.tldr: A hierarchical network model adds subgroups within latent attributes and improves link prediction on social and biological networks.

paragraphs: Large Markov decision processes can be difficult to solve because the space of possible situations grows too large to handle directly. Approximate dynamic programming addresses this through approximation. This paper proposes a class of methods that chooses approximations by minimizing a pessimistic bound on policy loss, tying the optimization target to decision quality.

The approach, called distributionally robust approximate dynamic programming, turns this task into an explicit optimization problem. The authors develop mathematical programming formulations and analyze their properties. Working with a pessimistic bound means optimizing a conservative assessment of how much performance a policy may lose, giving the approximation procedure a directly relevant objective.

The theoretical results provide convergence guarantees and error bounds measured using an L1 norm, improving on the guarantees of existing approximate dynamic programming methods discussed by the authors. Benchmark experiments also show good performance. Together, these findings suggest that the conservative optimization formulation can offer useful practical behavior alongside stronger mathematical guarantees.
icml-2012-approximate-dynamic-programmin.tldr: Distributionally robust approximate dynamic programming minimizes a pessimistic policy-loss bound and provides convergence guarantees with good benchmark performance.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether social connections help predict how users rate items. Social websites contain both material that users interact with and information about their social circles. The challenge is to combine these sources while learning how much each contributes to recommendations.

The authors propose a hierarchical Bayesian model that joins topic modeling with probabilistic matrix factorization of social networks. It learns hidden topics and social information from training data, along with their importance for collaborative filtering. This makes the contribution of social information something the model estimates, rather than a fixed judgment supplied beforehand.

Experiments on two large datasets report more effective recommendations than the state-of-the-art approaches compared. The results also suggest that social circles influence judgments about useful information more strongly than personal taste: bookmarking on Delicious and music preferences on Lastfm provide the examples. This is an empirical finding from the studied settings, highlighting that social information's predictive value can depend on the kind of preference being modeled.
icml-2012-collaborative-topic-regression.tldr: A Bayesian recommender jointly learns topics and social factors, improving recommendations while revealing differences in social influence across preference types.

paragraphs: Expectation Maximization is used to fit Gaussian mixture models, whose components represent different parts of a data distribution. Component overlap is already known to affect its convergence speed. This paper examines another factor: how unevenly the mixture's total weight is distributed across components.

The authors show that, when components have some overlap, EM converges more slowly as the range of mixing coefficients increases. The qualification about overlap matters: the result concerns the interaction between overlapping components and unequal weights. It helps explain why fitting can become slow when some components account for much more of the mixture than others.

To address this behavior, the paper proposes a deterministic anti-annealing algorithm and reports a substantial improvement in convergence speed for such mixtures. It compares the method with ordinary EM, LBFGS, and Conjugate Gradient. The authors also develop a related approach for Dirichlet process mixture fitting and demonstrate advantages over conventional variational Bayesian fitting, extending the proposed strategy to another mixture-model setting.
icml-2012-convergence-of-the-em-algorith.tldr: Unequal mixture weights slow EM when components overlap, and a deterministic anti-annealing method substantially accelerates fitting in this setting.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to measure dependence between random variables by applying Maximum Mean Discrepancy to the copula of their joint distribution. The copula-based formulation focuses on how variables relate to one another, providing a basis for measuring dependence through their relative ordering.

A central proven property is invariance under strictly increasing transformations of individual variables. Such transformations preserve ordering, and the dependence measure stays unchanged. The estimator uses only rank statistics, is consistent, and is robust to outliers. These properties matter when dependence should reflect relationships without being altered by an order-preserving change in how a variable is expressed.

The authors also derive upper bounds on the convergence rate and develop independence tests. Experiments with real and toy datasets illustrate applications to feature selection and low-dimensional representations of distributions. The contribution combines a dependence measure with statistical guarantees and practical uses, rather than offering only an empirical score for comparing variables.
icml-2012-copula-based-kernel-dependency.tldr: A copula-based kernel dependence measure uses ranks, resists outliers, and remains unchanged under strictly increasing transformations of individual variables.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of features can make data easier to work with, but the resulting representation still needs to preserve distinctions relevant to prediction. This paper introduces local discriminative Gaussian dimensionality reduction, or LDG, a supervised method that learns a linear mapping using information local to each training point.

The mapping is chosen so that similar examples can be distinguished from dissimilar ones. Although classification is the main setting studied, the method can also use training data supplied with similarity or dissimilarity constraints. Its local perspective guides the construction of a single linear representation, connecting neighborhood-level distinctions to the overall reduction in dimensionality.

Experiments show that LDG outperforms the compared state-of-the-art linear reduction techniques when the original data has many features. The authors also adapt it to transfer learning and report good performance when training and test distributions differ. These findings support its usefulness for high-dimensional supervised problems and for the distribution-shift settings examined in the paper.
icml-2012-dimensionality-reduction-by-lo.tldr: LDG learns a linear low-dimensional representation from local similarity information and performs well on high-dimensional classification and transfer-learning tasks.

paragraphs: Sparse learning seeks explanations that use relatively few active quantities. L1 regularization is a popular way to encourage this, but the paper asks whether its popularity translates into strong prediction on unseen data. The investigation focuses on unsupervised latent-variable models, where hidden factors explain observed data.

The authors develop and compare factor models using L1 minimization, Bayesian versions of L1-style sparsity, and Bayesian spike-and-slab distributions. The last approach encourages a stronger, L0-like distinction between inactive and active values. It also represents uncertainty and avoids unnecessarily shrinking nonzero values, addressing two aspects of estimation alongside the desire for sparsity.

Across several datasets and varied conditions, the spike-and-slab methods outperform L1 minimization in predictive performance, including under a computational budget. The authors also find that L1 can underperform dramatically in these comparisons. The findings motivate reconsidering L1 as a default for sparsity-dependent applications, particularly when generalization matters; they establish an empirical advantage across the studied conditions rather than a universal ranking of sparse methods.
icml-2012-evaluating-bayesian-and-l1-app.tldr: Bayesian spike-and-slab factor models outperform L1 minimization across the studied datasets, including when computation is constrained.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network includes choosing its structure: which variables connect to which others. Existing globally optimal structure-learning techniques had been developed around generative scores. This paper instead targets a discriminative score, the probabilistic soft margin, making structure selection directly relevant to classification.

The proposed exact method combines branch-and-bound search with a linear programming framework. It maintains a usable solution throughout the search and supplies worst-case bounds on how far that solution could be from optimal. This separates the ability to return an intermediate answer from the eventual goal of finding the globally best structure under the chosen score.

The authors introduce ordering constraints that enforce the absence of directed cycles. These constraints give a compact representation that general-purpose optimization methods can handle. Classification experiments show clear improvements over generatively trained network structures and competitive performance with support vector machines. The work therefore connects exact structural optimization to a classification-oriented objective while making the quality of intermediate solutions assessable.
icml-2012-exact-maximum-margin-structure.tldr: An exact optimization method learns Bayesian network structures for classification while maintaining intermediate solutions with worst-case suboptimality bounds.

paragraphs: When several related prediction tasks each have little training data, sharing information can improve generalization. The difficulty is deciding how the tasks are related. A fixed assumption about their relationship may be inappropriate, and the right form of sharing is rarely known before learning begins.

The paper introduces a generative model in which each task's weight vector comes from a nonparametric mixture of nonparametric factor analyzers. This supplies a flexible model for the hidden structure connecting tasks. It includes many previously studied task structures as special cases while also allowing more general relationships, broadening the ways parameters can be shared.

An efficient variational inference algorithm makes the model usable for learning. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets cover both regression and classification and support the method's effectiveness. The main contribution is to make task relatedness something the model can learn more flexibly, reducing dependence on a single relationship pattern fixed in advance.
icml-2012-flexible-modeling-of-latent-ta.tldr: A flexible Bayesian multitask model learns hidden relationships among tasks instead of requiring one fixed form of parameter sharing.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can benefit from using a small, useful subset of available features. One approach encourages sparsity through L1 regularization. This paper investigates an alternative: greedy algorithms that add features incrementally, adapting variants of orthogonal matching pursuit to reinforcement learning.

The authors analyze these variants and compare them experimentally with existing L1-regularized methods. Their theory shows that sparse recovery fails in a setting that might initially seem natural. However, a variant called OMP-BRM offers promising recovery guarantees under certain assumptions on the feature dictionary. The assumptions are essential to the positive result; the paper does not establish recovery for arbitrary collections of features.

A different variant, OMP-TD, performs better than prior methods in both approximation accuracy and computational efficiency on several benchmark problems. The theoretical and empirical strengths thus belong to distinct variants. Together, the results show why greedy feature selection deserves attention in reinforcement learning, while also demonstrating that guarantees from sparse learning require care when transferred into this setting.
icml-2012-greedy-algorithms-for-sparse-r.tldr: Greedy feature selection offers promising reinforcement-learning results, with conditional guarantees for OMP-BRM and strong benchmark performance for OMP-TD.

paragraphs: Models that adapt their parameters locally can represent changing relationships, but their estimates often have high variance. Locally weighted regression is one example motivating this paper. The authors propose reducing that variance by learning both a transformed space for the model and the locally adapted parameters within that space.

The central idea is to estimate these two parts together: the representation in which adaptation happens and the parameters that express the local behavior. This makes the representation itself part of the estimation problem. The paper introduces a formulation for this joint learning approach and develops it in the setting of models whose relationships change over time.

For a time-varying sparse network, the authors develop an algorithm that learns a collection of bases used to approximate the changing network. Each basis represents an archetypal sparse network structure. These learned structures provide a way to describe variation over time, and an extension allows the bases to be specific to individual tasks.

The paper reports empirical results on synthetic datasets and an EEG classification task for a brain–computer interface. These applications examine the proposed approach in both generated data and a classification setting. The abstract identifies variance reduction as the motivation, but does not state the direction or size of the empirical performance differences.
icml-2012-improved-estimation-in-time-va.tldr: The paper proposes jointly learning a model’s representation and locally adapted parameters to reduce variance, with an algorithm for approximating changing sparse networks.

paragraphs: A decision tree is built by choosing questions that divide the data into informative groups. Many tree-learning methods score candidate questions using information gain, which estimates how much a split reveals about the prediction target. The quality of that estimate therefore affects which branches the learning procedure creates.

The paper identifies bias in commonly used information-gain estimation procedures. It replaces their underlying entropy estimates with improved estimators, addressing discrete entropy for classification and differential entropy for regression. The intervention changes how candidate splits are evaluated while retaining the familiar idea of selecting informative questions.

The authors report that these modifications produce better trees and improve predictive performance. They also describe the changes as straightforward to implement in decision-tree code. This matters because a widely used component of tree training can influence the final model even when the surrounding learning procedure is unchanged. The contribution focuses on improving that statistical estimate rather than introducing an entirely new family of predictive models.
icml-2012-improved-information-gain-esti.tldr: Improved entropy estimators reduce bias in split scoring and yield decision trees with better predictive performance.

paragraphs: Matching objects between two sets often leads to a quadratic assignment problem, a difficult optimization task. This paper asks whether solving such problems can become easier when they repeatedly arise from the same application and correct matchings are available for some previous instances.

The proposed method learns parameters of a modified objective function from those solved examples. It uses the algebraic structure of permutations, which encode possible assignments, together with methods for optimizing over the symmetric group in Fourier space. The learning component brings application-specific information into the objective, while the harmonic-analysis component supplies machinery for handling the space of matchings.

Experiments show that the approach can substantially outperform existing methods in practical domains. The result is tied to the paper's source of additional information: related instances from one application and known solutions for training. Its contribution is a way to use that recurring structure to accelerate matching, rather than a claim that arbitrary quadratic assignment problems become easy.
icml-2012-incorporating-domain-knowledge.tldr: Learning from solved matching problems in the same application helps accelerate quadratic assignment through permutation-based harmonic analysis.

paragraphs: Metric learning seeks a distance rule that makes useful distinctions between examples. Seraph learns such a rule from both labeled and unlabeled data pairs using an information-theoretic objective. It does not depend on the manifold assumption commonly used to connect unlabeled data to the learning task.

The method combines entropy maximization for labeled pairs with entropy minimization for unlabeled pairs, integrating supervised and unsupervised information in one formulation. Under the specified probabilistic model, it also produces sparsity in both the posterior distribution and the resulting projection matrix. The authors call this combination hyper-sparsity and connect it to strong discrimination even in noisy environments.

Seraph is optimized through an EM-like procedure with an analytical E-step and a smooth, convex M-step. These properties support efficient and stable optimization of the proposed formulation. Experiments compare favorably with many established metric-learning methods. The contribution combines a way to use unlabeled pairs, a sparse learned representation, and a tractable optimization procedure within one model.
icml-2012-information-theoretic-semi-sup.tldr: Seraph combines entropy objectives and sparsity to learn discriminative metrics from labeled and unlabeled pairs without relying on a manifold assumption.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer a regular expression from a collection of strings so that it resembles one a human expert would write. Its practical motivation is email administration, where postmasters create patterns to describe spam campaigns and decide which patterns they are confident enough to blacklist.

Training examples pair batches of messages with regular expressions supplied by an expert postmaster. The authors formulate the task as structured prediction: the output is an expression with internal structure, rather than a single category. They introduce a suitable loss function, derive a decoder for producing expressions, and formulate the corresponding optimization problem.

A case study with an email service examines the approach in its intended application. The target is expert-like campaign descriptions, so learning from the postmaster's chosen expressions is central to the problem definition. The work provides a learning formulation and algorithmic components for automating this pattern-writing task, with the case study connecting those components to email-service practice.
icml-2012-learning-to-identify-regular-e.tldr: Structured prediction learns to generate expert-like regular expressions for email campaigns from message batches paired with postmaster-written patterns.

paragraphs: MAP inference seeks the best joint assignment under a model's energy function, and general instances remain difficult. Linear programming relaxations provide one route to approximate solutions. This paper draws on a quadratic programming relaxation to modify how the relaxed problem represents relationships between variables.

The proposed objective penalizes a Kullback-Leibler divergence between pairwise auxiliary quantities in the linear relaxation and products of unary quantities associated with the quadratic formulation. In effect, it discourages disagreement between these two representations of pairwise behavior. The result links information from the LP and QP viewpoints within a new MAP relaxation.

The authors develop two efficient algorithms for variants of this formulation, using belief propagation and dual decomposition as components. Their objective is nonconvex, so the reported contribution is not an exact global solution guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show substantial improvements over the LP relaxation, demonstrating that the additional consistency penalty can improve the solutions obtained in the studied problems.
icml-2012-lpqp-for-map-putting-lp-solver.tldr: A KL-divergence penalty connects LP and QP representations for MAP inference and substantially improves solutions over the LP relaxation in experiments.

paragraphs: F-measures are commonly used when class frequencies are uneven, but learning to optimize them can follow different routes. Empirical utility maximization chooses a classifier for strong F-measure on training data. The decision-theoretic route first learns a probabilistic model and then chooses labels to maximize expected F-measure.

The paper examines the theoretical foundations and connections between these approaches, alongside experiments on synthetic and real datasets. With accurate models and large training and test sets, the results suggest asymptotic equivalence. This is a qualified conclusion about a large-data setting, rather than a claim that the methods behave identically in every application.

Their practical strengths also appear to differ. Empirical utility maximization seems more robust when the model is misspecified. With a good probabilistic model, the decision-theoretic approach appears better at handling rare classes and a common domain-adaptation scenario. The findings make model quality and the prediction setting central considerations when choosing how to optimize F-measure.
icml-2012-optimizing-f-measure-a-tale-of.tldr: Two approaches to optimizing F-measure appear asymptotically equivalent with accurate models, but show different practical strengths under misspecification and rare classes.

paragraphs: A single misclassification rate compresses all classification errors into one number. A confusion matrix retains information about which classes are mistaken for which others. This paper develops generalization guarantees around that richer description of error for a Gibbs classifier in a multiclass setting.

The authors use matrix concentration inequalities to derive two PAC-Bayesian bounds. These bounds place an upper limit on the classifier's true confusion risk using its empirical risk plus an additional term. That term depends on the number of training examples in each class, making class-specific sample availability part of the guarantee.

The importance of the result is the change in what receives theoretical protection: performance is assessed through confusion behavior rather than only an aggregate error rate. The authors describe these as the first PAC-Bayesian bounds based on confusion matrices, to their knowledge. The contribution is theoretical, providing a way to relate observed multiclass errors to population-level confusion risk while accounting for the training evidence available for individual classes.
icml-2012-pac-bayesian-generalization-bo.tldr: New PAC-Bayesian bounds control multiclass confusion risk using empirical confusion risk and the number of training examples in each class.

paragraphs: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods can appear to follow very different recipes. This paper shows that almost all nonparametric methods in this area can be expressed through a shared procedure: minimize a regularized loss, then truncate singular values. The common formulation makes their design choices easier to separate and compare.

The loss describes what the representation should preserve or fit, while the regularizer expresses additional preferences about its structure. Treating these as separate components reveals gaps among existing methods. The authors use this perspective to identify a useful new loss for manifold unfolding, showing how the framework can suggest new constructions.

A central contribution is a set of convex regularizers that jointly encourage larger distances and lower rank. These regularizers can be paired with any loss, so their role is not confined to one particular fitting objective. The paper's value lies in both unifying existing approaches and supplying reusable components for building dimensionality-reduction methods.
icml-2012-regularizers-versus-losses-for.tldr: A shared loss-and-regularizer formulation unifies dimensionality-reduction methods and yields convex regularizers combining distance maximization with rank reduction.

paragraphs: Exploration helps an agent learn an unknown environment, but visiting unfamiliar states can be dangerous in physical systems. Many exploration methods rely on ergodicity: suitable actions give a nonzero chance of reaching any state from any other in finite time. Physical damage can make that assumption unrealistic.

The paper proposes a safety formulation that can be understood as enforcing this kind of reachability. Imposing the constraint exactly is NP-hard, so the authors develop an efficient approximation. Its optimization constraints restrict the search to guaranteed safe policies, while its objective encourages exploration. The safety guarantee comes with the possibility of suboptimal exploration.

The framework can incorporate exploration bonuses used by most previously proposed exploration methods by placing them in the objective. Experiments show safe exploration in state spaces where classical methods become stuck. The contribution is a way to pursue informative behavior within a guaranteed safe policy set, while explicitly acknowledging the computational difficulty of enforcing the original constraint exactly.
icml-2012-safe-exploration-in-markov-dec.tldr: An efficient approximation restricts exploration to guaranteed safe policies, potentially sacrificing optimality while avoiding failures seen with classical exploration.

paragraphs: A classifier's training data may contain different class proportions from the data it encounters later. That mismatch can introduce substantial estimation bias. If the test-set proportions were known, reweighting or resampling training instances would provide a systematic way to correct for the changed class balance.

The paper addresses the harder case in which test-domain labels are unavailable. It estimates the test-set class ratios by matching probability distributions of training and test inputs. This uses information in the unlabeled test data to infer an aggregate property of the test population: how common each class is.

Experiments demonstrate the utility of the proposed approach. The contribution targets the missing quantity needed for class-balance correction, rather than assuming it is already available. Within the class-prior-change setting, distribution matching provides a route from observed input data to estimated class proportions, connecting unlabeled test examples to the reweighting or resampling strategies that could use those estimates.
icml-2012-semi-supervised-learning-of-cl.tldr: Matching training and test input distributions estimates test-set class proportions without requiring labels from the test domain.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear systems whose coefficients are observed with noise, motivated by estimating value functions in reinforcement learning. An estimated solution can fit the noisy system yet leave an error in the true system. The authors evaluate that error using a matrix-weighted two-norm of the residual under the unknown true coefficients.

They consider penalized estimators with two objectives: one squares the residual norm computed from noisy coefficients, while the other leaves it unsquared. For both, they propose data-dependent choices of regularization parameters that avoid splitting the data. This gives a theoretically supported way to set the penalty using the available observations.

The analysis derives deterministic error bounds expressed in terms of coefficient-estimation errors. This separates the behavior of the estimator from the probabilistic analysis of how those coefficient errors arise. The authors then apply the results to linear value-function estimation, obtaining new bounds and insights for reinforcement learning. The separation makes the general inverse-problem analysis directly useful for that motivating application.
icml-2012-statistical-linear-estimation-.tldr: Data-dependent regularization choices and deterministic error bounds improve the theoretical treatment of noisy linear systems and reinforcement-learning value estimation.

paragraphs: Many learning problems minimize convex losses that are not smooth, making optimization a central concern. This paper introduces Accelerated Nonsmooth Stochastic Gradient Descent, or ANSGD. It uses structure present in common nonsmooth loss functions to accelerate stochastic optimization.

The authors establish optimal convergence rates for a class of problems that includes support vector machines. They report an O(1/t) rate, where t indexes optimization progress: the convergence bound decreases inversely with t. The stated guarantee belongs to the structured problem class analyzed, so the relevant contribution is exploiting that structure to obtain the fast rate.

Empirical comparisons support the theoretical findings, with ANSGD substantially outperforming earlier subgradient methods, including SGD. The paper presents the method as the first stochastic algorithm to attain the stated optimal rate for nonsmooth loss minimization. Its practical message is that recognizing structure within a nonsmooth objective can materially change how quickly a stochastic learning algorithm converges.
icml-2012-stochastic-smoothing-for-nonsm.tldr: ANSGD exploits structured nonsmooth losses to achieve optimal O(1/t) convergence for a problem class including SVMs and outperforms earlier subgradient methods experimentally.

paragraphs: Mean-field variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior with a collection of factorized distributions. It fits that approximation by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood. Doing so requires expectations of the model's log joint likelihood, and those integrals are not always available in closed form.

A traditional response is to introduce additional lower-bound approximations for the difficult terms. This paper instead proposes stochastic optimization to optimize the variational lower bound directly. The authors present the method as applicable across models, providing a general route around the need to evaluate every required integral analytically.

The stochastic search uses control variates to reduce noise in gradient estimates. Existing lower bounds can contribute to this variance-reduction mechanism, giving them a useful role even when they no longer replace the objective being optimized. Demonstrations on logistic regression and the hierarchical Dirichlet process illustrate the approach. The contribution is a general inference strategy that combines direct optimization of the variational objective with tools for making noisy gradient search more manageable.
icml-2012-variational-bayesian-inference.tldr: Stochastic search with variance-reducing control variates directly optimizes variational lower bounds when required integrals lack closed forms.

paragraphs: Audio source separation benefits from modeling both spectral patterns and how sounds change over time. Non-negative matrix factorization captures spectral structure, but neglects temporal dynamics. Non-negative factorial hidden Markov models add that temporal dimension and improve separation, at the cost of inference complexity that grows exponentially with the number of sources.

The paper introduces a Bayesian variant of this temporal model designed for efficient variational inference. The proposed algorithm's complexity grows linearly with the number of sound sources. This addresses the computational burden of the factorial structure while retaining a model that represents temporal behavior.

The authors report separation performance comparable to exact inference in the original model, with substantially faster computation. Typical model configurations show roughly a thirtyfold speed increase. That figure describes the reported configurations rather than every possible use. The results show that approximate inference in the Bayesian variant can preserve comparable separation performance while making multi-source temporal modeling much more computationally manageable.
icml-2012-variational-inference-in-non-n.tldr: Variational inference makes a Bayesian temporal audio-separation model scale linearly in source count, with comparable performance and roughly 30× speedups in typical configurations.
